structure.rationale: The 14-chapter order comes from the requester's syllabus (issue #187) and is kept as given. It runs from the running database (architecture, undo/redo, multitenant), through building and securing the environment, to protecting data and recovering, then observing and tuning, and finally changing and keeping it available. Each part relies on vocabulary from the one before; the order of the later chapters follows the syllabus. Baseline release: Oracle Database 19c, a long-term release still widely run in production, with Premier Support reported through 2029 and Extended Support through 2032. 23ai has been renamed 26ai, and its Extended Support date was not yet announced when checked. Version-specific and licensing-dependent features (e.g. AWR/ASH under the Diagnostics Pack) are flagged per chapter. Each chapter follows the notes' shape: problem, mechanism, tools, worked example, lab, injected failure, remediation, validation/rollback, checklist, with one running order-processing case study. The book is narrated in the Thing Explainer persona, so real terms appear once in quotes beside a plain description.
structure.audience: Readers who already know SQL, relational databases and basic transactions, and want to run Oracle in production; SQL fundamentals and installation walkthroughs are out of scope.

claims.text: A database is the set of files on disk (datafiles, control files, online redo logs); an instance is the memory (SGA) plus background processes that opens and serves it.

The SGA is shared memory holding the database buffer cache, shared pool (including library cache), redo log buffer and more; each server process also has private PGA memory (e.g. sort and hash work areas).

SQL processing runs parse, execute, fetch (fetch for queries). A soft parse reuses a cursor already in the library cache; a hard parse builds a new plan and is costlier. Bind variables let statements share cursors.
Server processes read blocks into the buffer cache; changes are made to cached blocks (making them dirty) and generate redo and undo; the change is not written to datafiles at that moment.

Changes are first described in the redo log buffer. On COMMIT, LGWR writes the buffer to the online redo log; the commit completes (the session waits on 'log file sync') once that write is done. DBWn writes dirty blocks later and lazily.
LGWR also writes when the buffer is a third full, every ~3 seconds, and before DBWn writes dirty blocks (write-ahead logging); concurrent commits can share one write (group commit).
Checkpoints (CKPT) advance a checkpoint position recorded in the control file and datafile headers; DBWn writes dirty blocks to move it forward. Checkpoint also happens at log switch.

Instance recovery after a crash is done automatically by SMON/at open: roll forward by applying redo from the checkpoint position to the end of the log (cache recovery), then roll back uncommitted transactions using undo (transaction recovery). Committed data survives because its redo reached disk.

Online redo log groups are written in a circular fashion; a group cannot be reused until its changes are checkpointed (and archived, if in ARCHIVELOG mode). Multiplexing members across disks guards against losing one copy.

The control file records the database name, datafile and redo log locations, checkpoint info and backup metadata; it is read at MOUNT. Startup stages: NOMOUNT (instance), MOUNT (control file), OPEN (datafiles and redo).
Dedicated server mode gives each session its own server process; shared server mode uses dispatchers and a pool. Main background processes: PMON/PMAN, SMON, DBWn, LGWR, CKPT, ARCn.
Useful views: V$INSTANCE, V$DATABASE, V$SGAINFO, V$PROCESS, V$SESSION, V$LOG, V$LOGFILE, V$CONTROLFILE, V$DATAFILE, V$SYSSTAT, V$SESSTAT, V$SQL, V$LOG_HISTORY.

snippets.code:
SELECT instance_name, status, database_status FROM v$instance;
SELECT name, log_mode, open_mode FROM v$database;

SELECT group#, sequence#, status, members FROM v$log;
SELECT group#, member FROM v$logfile;

SELECT n.name, s.value FROM v$mystat s JOIN v$statname n USING (statistic#)
WHERE n.name IN ('redo size','user commits','session logical reads');

ALTER SYSTEM CHECKPOINT;
ALTER SYSTEM SWITCH LOGFILE;
snippets.note: lab only; do not run at busy times in production

pitfalls: Believing COMMIT writes data blocks to datafiles; it writes redo.
Calling the instance the database (or the reverse) when tracing a fault.
Sizing redo logs so small that log switches and checkpoints come every few seconds.
Treating 'log file sync' waits as a DBWn problem; they point at LGWR and redo disk latency.
Forcing checkpoints or log switches in production 'to be safe'.

claims.text: The System Change Number (SCN) is a database-wide logical clock that increases with each commit; Oracle stamps changes and read snapshots with SCNs to order events.

Undo records how to reverse a change and serves read consistency, rollback and recovery of uncommitted work; redo records how to re-make a change and serves roll-forward recovery. A change generates both; undo is itself protected by redo.
Readers do not block writers and writers do not block readers: a query sees data as of its snapshot SCN, rebuilding older block versions by applying undo to a copy of the block (consistent read).

Default read consistency is statement-level: each query sees data as of the SCN at its start. Transaction-level consistency needs SET TRANSACTION READ ONLY or ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE (the latter can raise ORA-08177). READ COMMITTED is the default isolation level.

Row locks are taken by INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/MERGE/SELECT FOR UPDATE and held until COMMIT or ROLLBACK. The transaction also takes a TX enqueue lock; a session wanting a locked row waits on that TX lock (wait event 'enq: TX - row lock contention'). Oracle has no lock escalation.

Blocking is found with V$SESSION (BLOCKING_SESSION, FINAL_BLOCKING_SESSION, WAIT_CLASS/EVENT, SQL_ID) and V$LOCK (TYPE, LMODE, REQUEST). Killing the blocker is ALTER SYSTEM KILL SESSION 'sid,serial#' and rolls back its work, which can itself take time.

Deadlock: two sessions each hold a row the other wants. Oracle detects it, rolls back the statement of one session (not the whole transaction), raises ORA-00060 and writes a trace file named in the alert log. The application must handle it. Common avoidable cause: unindexed foreign keys and inconsistent lock order.

With automatic undo management, undo lives in an undo tablespace. Active (uncommitted) undo is never overwritten; unexpired undo (committed, younger than retention) is kept if space allows; expired undo is reused first. UNDO_RETENTION is a target in seconds, not a guarantee, unless the tablespace has RETENTION GUARANTEE (which can make DML fail with ORA-30036 when undo is full).

ORA-01555 'snapshot too old' occurs when a query needs undo that has been overwritten, so it cannot rebuild the block as of its snapshot. Causes: queries running longer than undo covers, undo too small for the change rate, or frequent commits reusing undo; also delayed block cleanout and fetching across commits. Fixes: tune the query, raise undo size/UNDO_RETENTION, avoid committing inside the loop that is reading.

V$UNDOSTAT keeps ten-minute rows with UNDOBLKS, TXNCOUNT, MAXQUERYLEN (longest query in seconds), MAXQUERYID, SSOLDERRCNT (ORA-01555 count) and NOSPACEERRCNT; with auto-tuned retention, TUNED_UNDORETENTION shows the retention in effect. The alert log records ORA-01555 with the SQL ID.
Flashback Query (SELECT ... AS OF TIMESTAMP/SCN) uses the same undo; how far back it reaches depends on undo retention.
Instance recovery uses redo to roll forward then undo to roll back uncommitted transactions; this ties this chapter to the previous one.

snippets.code:
SELECT CURRENT_SCN FROM v$database;
SELECT dbms_flashback.get_system_change_number FROM dual;
snippets.note: 19c; the latter needs EXECUTE on DBMS_FLASHBACK

snippets.code:
SELECT sid, serial#, blocking_session, final_blocking_session, event, seconds_in_wait, sql_id
FROM v$session WHERE blocking_session IS NOT NULL;

SELECT begin_time, undoblks, txncount, maxquerylen, ssolderrcnt, nospaceerrcnt, tuned_undoretention
FROM v$undostat ORDER BY begin_time DESC FETCH FIRST 12 ROWS ONLY;

SELECT tablespace_name, retention FROM dba_tablespaces WHERE contents='UNDO';
SHOW PARAMETER undo
SELECT status, SUM(bytes)/1024/1024 mb FROM dba_undo_extents GROUP BY status;

pitfalls: Thinking COMMIT frequency is free: committing inside a loop that reads the same table invites ORA-01555 and breaks atomicity.
Believing readers wait for writers (true in many other databases, not Oracle).
Setting UNDO_RETENTION huge without sizing the undo tablespace.
Killing the blocking session without checking what it was doing; its rollback may take as long as its work did.
Treating deadlock ORA-00060 as an Oracle bug; the application's lock order is the cause.
Using RETENTION GUARANTEE casually: it can make writers fail instead of readers.
Conflating undo (reverse) with redo (replay).

claims.text: A multitenant container database (CDB) holds one root (CDB$ROOT, CON_ID 1), one seed PDB (PDB$SEED, CON_ID 2, read-only template) and zero or more pluggable databases (PDBs). One instance (one SGA, one set of background processes, shared redo and control files) serves all containers.

Each PDB has its own data dictionary for its own objects, its own SYSTEM/SYSAUX and application tablespaces and datafiles, and its own temp; metadata for Oracle-supplied objects lives in the root and is linked.
Application containers (12.2+) are a special PDB kind: an application root plus application PDBs that share application-owned common objects. Not the same as ordinary user PDBs.

Common users exist in all containers and are created in the root; common user names must start with C## (or the value of COMMON_USER_PREFIX) unless Oracle-supplied. Local users exist in one PDB only and cannot be created in the root. A privilege granted locally applies only in that container; granted with CONTAINER=ALL from the root it applies in all.
ALTER SESSION SET CONTAINER=<name> moves a session with proper privileges between root and PDBs without reconnecting; SHOW CON_NAME or SYS_CONTEXT('USERENV','CON_NAME') reports the current container.

Each PDB gets a default service with the PDB's name that the listener registers; clients should connect to a PDB through its service name, not a SID. Extra services can be added per PDB (e.g. DBMS_SERVICE or srvctl).

After a CDB restart, PDBs are left MOUNTED unless their state was saved with ALTER PLUGGABLE DATABASE ... SAVE STATE (available since 12.1.0.2). Opening: ALTER PLUGGABLE DATABASE name OPEN; closing: CLOSE IMMEDIATE.

CREATE PLUGGABLE DATABASE from the seed needs an ADMIN USER clause; that user becomes a local administrator in the new PDB. FILE_NAME_CONVERT (or Oracle Managed Files / CREATE_FILE_DEST) decides where the files go.

CREATE PLUGGABLE DATABASE new FROM existing clones a PDB. A hot clone (source stays open read write) needs local undo mode and ARCHIVELOG mode; otherwise the source must be open read only. Remote clone uses a database link (FROM pdb@dblink).

Unplug writes an XML manifest (or .pdb archive) describing the PDB: ALTER PLUGGABLE DATABASE x UNPLUG INTO 'file'; then DROP PLUGGABLE DATABASE x KEEP DATAFILES. Plugging in uses CREATE PLUGGABLE DATABASE ... USING 'file' with COPY, MOVE or NOCOPY; DBMS_PDB.CHECK_PLUG_COMPATIBILITY checks compatibility first; PDB_PLUG_IN_VIOLATIONS records mismatches.

Views: V$CONTAINERS, V$PDBS, CDB_PDBS (list containers); CDB_* dictionary views show data for all containers when queried from the root, while DBA_* views show only the current container. Most V$ views have a CON_ID column.

Parameters: most initialization parameters are CDB-wide, set in the root; those flagged ISPDB_MODIFIABLE in V$SYSTEM_PARAMETER can be set inside a PDB. ALTER SYSTEM SET ... CONTAINER=ALL|CURRENT scopes the change.

Redo logs, control files and (in shared undo mode) the undo tablespace are CDB-level; in local undo mode each PDB has its own undo tablespace. Backups: RMAN can back up the whole CDB or single PDBs; PDB point-in-time recovery exists. Resource Manager (CDB plans) and per-PDB limits such as MAX_PDB_STORAGE share resources between PDBs.

Licensing: on Enterprise Edition 19c up to three user-created PDBs per CDB are allowed without the Multitenant option; the software does not enforce the count. 12c/18c allowed one. Edition rules for Standard Edition 2 are reported inconsistently by secondary sources; confirm in the Licensing Information manual.
Cloning a PDB into a Data Guard primary can leave the standby without the new PDB's datafiles; Oracle suggests a transient clone with STANDBYS=NONE for such cases.
Non-CDB architecture is deprecated since 12.1 and desupported from 21c; 19c still allows non-CDB.

snippets.code:
SHOW CON_NAME
SELECT con_id, name, open_mode FROM v$pdbs ORDER BY con_id;

snippets.note: paths are examples; omit convert with OMF

snippets.code:
CREATE PLUGGABLE DATABASE orderstest FROM ordersdev;
ALTER PLUGGABLE DATABASE orderstest OPEN;
snippets.note: source must be read only unless local undo + ARCHIVELOG

snippets.code:
ALTER SESSION SET CONTAINER = orderstest;
SELECT sys_context('USERENV','CON_NAME') FROM dual;

CREATE USER c##ops IDENTIFIED BY "<password>" CONTAINER=ALL;
GRANT CREATE SESSION TO c##ops CONTAINER=ALL;

pitfalls: Running ALTER SYSTEM or a grant in the root and thinking it only touched one PDB (or the reverse).
PDBs left MOUNTED after restart because state was never saved.
Connecting by SID or to the root service when the app needs the PDB service.
Hot clone refused because the CDB is in shared undo mode or NOARCHIVELOG.
Creating a 4th PDB on Enterprise Edition without the Multitenant option; the software won't stop you.
Cloning a production PDB copies production data; mask before giving it to dev.

claims.text: ALTER SYSTEM SET ... SCOPE= takes MEMORY (running instance only, lost at restart), SPFILE (next startup only) or BOTH (default when started with an SPFILE). Static parameters can only use SCOPE=SPFILE.

Startup passes through NOMOUNT (instance: memory and background processes, parameter file read), MOUNT (control file opened) and OPEN (datafiles and redo opened). ALTER SYSTEM is usable from NOMOUNT on.

Shutdown modes: NORMAL waits for all sessions to leave; TRANSACTIONAL waits for open transactions; IMMEDIATE rolls back active transactions and disconnects; ABORT does no cleanup and needs instance recovery at next startup.
An SPFILE can be created from a PFILE (CREATE SPFILE FROM PFILE) and back (CREATE PFILE FROM SPFILE) without starting the instance. The SPFILE is binary and must not be hand-edited.

On Linux, the oracle-database-preinstall-19c package (Oracle Linux/RHEL family) creates the oracle user and oinstall/dba groups and sets kernel parameters and shell limits; practitioner guides show fs.file-max=6815744, aio-max-nr=1048576, nofile and nproc limits for the oracle user.

DBCA can create a database non-interactively with dbca -silent -createDatabase, taking template, gdbname, sid, character set and createAsContainerDatabase options; a response file can hold the same answers.

ORACLE_HOME (the software tree) and ORACLE_SID (the instance name) are environment variables; a DB is bound to the home that created it, so patching strategy depends on the home layout. The database name, instance name and service name are different things.

V$PARAMETER / V$SYSTEM_PARAMETER show running values; V$SPPARAMETER shows what the SPFILE holds; a mismatch is configuration drift between memory and file. ISSYS_MODIFIABLE says IMMEDIATE, DEFERRED or FALSE.
In a CDB, init parameters are set at the CDB level; a PDB may override those marked ISPDB_MODIFIABLE. Multitenant is the only architecture for new databases from 21c.

snippets.code: CREATE PFILE='/stage/init_backup.ora' FROM SPFILE;
dbca -silent -createDatabase -templateName General_Purpose.dbc -gdbname ORCL -sid ORCL -characterSet AL32UTF8 -createAsContainerDatabase true -numberOfPDBs 1 -pdbName orders
snippets.note: passwords supplied via prompt/response file, not shown; verify options with dbca -help

pitfalls: SCOPE=MEMORY change silently vanishes at restart; SCOPE=SPFILE does not take effect now.
Hand-editing init.ora while the instance uses an SPFILE does nothing.
Static parameter set with default SCOPE fails with ORA-02095.
Different ORACLE_HOME or ORACLE_SID in a cron shell than in your login shell.
Passwords typed on a command line show up in process lists and shell history.

claims.text: A client connection goes to a listener (default TCP 1521), which hands it to a service; the client names a service in a connect descriptor (HOST, PORT, SERVICE_NAME).
The listener works with no listener.ora using defaults (TCP 1521); database services register dynamically with it via the LREG process, with no manual listener.ora entries.

LOCAL_LISTENER points registration at a non-default local listener; REMOTE_LISTENER registers with listeners elsewhere. ALTER SYSTEM REGISTER forces registration now. Registration can lag up to about a minute after startup.

Prefer SERVICE_NAME over SID in connect descriptors: services are logical names (a database can have many) and each PDB has its own default service named after the PDB; SID connects only to an instance and cannot reach a PDB.

Name resolution methods: Easy Connect (host:port/service), local naming (tnsnames.ora, found via TNS_ADMIN or $ORACLE_HOME/network/admin), directory naming (LDAP). NAMES.DIRECTORY_PATH in sqlnet.ora sets the order.

Dedicated server: one server process per session. Shared server: dispatchers (DISPATCHERS parameter) pass requests to a pool of shared server processes (SHARED_SERVERS); SERVER=DEDICATED in the descriptor forces a dedicated process. Long-running or admin work should use dedicated.

Diagnostic ladder: lsnrctl status/services on the server shows the listener and registered services; tnsping tests the listener and name resolution only (not authentication or the database); sqlplus user@//host:port/service tests the full path.

ORA-12541 TNS:no listener: nothing is answering at the host:port tried (listener down, wrong port, or blocked). ORA-12514: the listener answered but does not know the requested service. ORA-12154: the name could not be resolved (client naming). ORA-12170: connect timeout, often a firewall dropping packets. ORA-01017: invalid username/password (authentication reached the database).

Native network encryption and integrity are set in sqlnet.ora (SQLNET.ENCRYPTION_SERVER/CLIENT, SQLNET.CRYPTO_CHECKSUM_*), with values ACCEPTED, REJECTED, REQUESTED, REQUIRED; TLS uses the TCPS protocol with a wallet and a TCPS listener endpoint (commonly port 2484 or 1522).

From the database side, connection pools hold many long-lived sessions; a pool bigger than the database's PROCESSES/SESSIONS limit gives ORA-00020 (maximum processes exceeded), and a connection storm (many new logons at once) is a listener and logon cost; the listener rate limit and QUEUESIZE can matter. Sessions are visible in V$SESSION with MACHINE, PROGRAM, SERVICE_NAME.

Local works but remote fails: a local BEQ/bequeath connection (no listener, using ORACLE_SID) bypasses the network entirely; so 'works on the server' proves the database is open and says nothing about the listener, service registration, host firewall or client naming.
A listener binding to 'localhost' or the wrong host name/IP (listener.ora HOST) accepts local but refuses remote connections; check with lsnrctl status and the OS (ss -ltn).

snippets.code:
lsnrctl status
lsnrctl services

tnsping //dbhost:1521/orders_svc
sqlplus app_user@//dbhost:1521/orders_svc
snippets.note: from the application host; Easy Connect syntax host:port/service

snippets.code:
ALTER SYSTEM SET local_listener='(ADDRESS=(PROTOCOL=TCP)(HOST=dbhost)(PORT=1521))' SCOPE=BOTH;
ALTER SYSTEM REGISTER;

ORDERS =
  (DESCRIPTION=
    (ADDRESS=(PROTOCOL=TCP)(HOST=dbhost)(PORT=1521))
    (CONNECT_DATA=(SERVICE_NAME=orders_svc)))

pitfalls: tnsping success does not prove login will work.
Using SID where only a PDB service exists.
Editing the wrong tnsnames.ora: TNS_ADMIN overrides the home's network/admin.
Listener started before the database: services missing until registration catches up; ALTER SYSTEM REGISTER.
Host firewall open on server but a network firewall in between drops packets silently: timeout, not refusal.
Pool max larger than PROCESSES.

claims.text: Space is nested: a block is the smallest unit of I/O; contiguous blocks form an extent; the extents of one object form a segment; segments live in a tablespace; a tablespace is stored in one or more datafiles. Default block size is 8 KB (DB_BLOCK_SIZE).

Tablespaces created in 19c are locally managed by default, with automatic segment space management (ASSM) as the usual choice for user data; the database keeps the free-space map in the datafile headers, not the data dictionary.

SYSTEM holds the data dictionary and SYSAUX holds auxiliary components (AWR, optimizer stats history and others); neither can be dropped or taken offline normally, and user data should not live in them. Set a default permanent tablespace so new users do not land in SYSTEM/USERS by accident.

A smallfile tablespace may have many datafiles, each limited to about 4 million blocks (about 32 GB at 8 KB). A bigfile tablespace has exactly one datafile that can hold about 4 billion blocks (about 32 TB at 8 KB). Bigfile moves the management unit to the tablespace but makes one file very large to back up and restore.

A datafile with AUTOEXTEND ON grows by NEXT until it reaches MAXSIZE (or the smallfile limit if UNLIMITED, 32768 MB at 8 KB blocks); after that, or when the filesystem or disk group is full, allocation fails with ORA-01653 (table) or ORA-01654/01655 (index/cluster).

A naive DBA_FREE_SPACE-based percentage can mislead: a file with autoextend and a large MAXSIZE has more headroom than it shows. DBA_TABLESPACE_USAGE_METRICS reports USED_PERCENT against the maximum possible size, which is the number to alert on.

Temporary tablespaces hold sort, hash, global-temporary-table and similar spill data in tempfiles; ORA-01652 means a temp segment could not be extended. Freed temp extents stay cached inside the tempfile for reuse, so the file stays large and DBA_TEMP_FREE_SPACE shows reuse room, not OS room. ALTER TABLESPACE temp SHRINK SPACE (optionally KEEP size) gives space back.

V$TEMPSEG_USAGE (and GV$ for clusters) shows which session and SQL are using temp now; V$SORT_USAGE is the older synonym-style view. The fix for ORA-01652 is to retry, add tempfile space or raise MAXSIZE, or fix the query that spilled.

Undo has its own tablespace (UNDO_TABLESPACE); its used space is governed by retention and active transactions (see Chapter 2), and V$UNDOSTAT shows its use. Undo and temp are not backed up like permanent data in the same way: tempfiles carry no needed data and can be recreated.

Deleting rows does not shrink the segment or the datafile: the high water mark stays. Space returns via ALTER TABLE ... ENABLE ROW MOVEMENT then SHRINK SPACE [CASCADE] (needs ASSM; online, takes brief locks at the end), ALTER TABLE ... MOVE, DEALLOCATE UNUSED (only space above the high water mark), or TRUNCATE.

ALTER DATABASE DATAFILE '...' RESIZE n can only go down to the end of the last used block; if a segment lives at the tail of the file, resize fails with ORA-03297 until that segment is moved or shrunk.

With the recycle bin on, DROP TABLE renames the table to BIN$... and its space stays charged to the tablespace until PURGE or until space pressure reclaims it; DROP ... PURGE or PURGE RECYCLEBIN / PURGE TABLESPACE frees it at once.

Datafiles can sit on a filesystem or in ASM disk groups. ASM stripes and mirrors extents across disks, with redundancy set per disk group (external, normal, high); with ASM, 'full' means the disk group (V$ASM_DISKGROUP FREE_MB / USABLE_FILE_MB), not a mount point. Oracle Managed Files (db_create_file_dest) lets the database name and place files itself.

In a CDB each PDB has its own tablespaces and datafiles (including its own SYSTEM/SYSAUX and, by default, local temp); a PDB can be capped with MAX_PDB_STORAGE and a separate temp limit with MAX_SHARED_TEMP_SIZE. Space queries must be run in the right container (DBA_ views show the current container; CDB_ views from root show all).

Capacity planning means sampling growth over time (e.g. segment sizes per week from DBA_SEGMENTS / DBA_HIST_SEG_STAT if licensed) and projecting days-to-full; AWR-based history needs the Diagnostics Pack on Enterprise Edition, so a plain scheduled snapshot table is the portable option.

snippets.code:
SELECT tablespace_name,
       ROUND(used_percent,1) used_pct,
       ROUND(tablespace_size*8192/1024/1024/1024,1) max_gb
  FROM dba_tablespace_usage_metrics
 ORDER BY used_percent DESC;
snippets.note: tablespace_size is in blocks of the tablespace; 8192 assumes an 8 KB block. Autoextend aware.
8192 assumes an 8 KB block. Instance-local; use GV$ on RAC.
Lab-style syntax; shrink needs ASSM; resize fails with ORA-03297 if data lies past the new end.

pitfalls: A 'tablespace 95% full' alert from a free-space join can be false when autoextend has headroom, and a '40% full' one can be false when the filesystem or disk group behind it is nearly full: the real limit is the smallest of MAXSIZE, the smallfile cap and the real disk.
Deleting rows frees space inside the segment, not in the datafile; people delete a lot and the file does not shrink.
Temp looks 100% used long after the query ended; that is reuse cache, not a leak. Look at V$TEMPSEG_USAGE before resizing.
Dropping a big table with the recycle bin on frees nothing until purged.
Shrinking or moving segments generates redo and undo and can fill the archive destination: space remediation can cause the next space incident.
Autoextend hides growth until the disk is full; set MAXSIZE on purpose.

claims.text: In Oracle a user owns a schema, the set of objects with the same name; a user can exist with no objects. A role is a named bundle of privileges; a profile is a named bundle of resource limits and password rules.

System privileges allow an action in the database (CREATE SESSION, CREATE TABLE, and the dangerous ANY family such as SELECT ANY TABLE); object privileges allow an action on one object (SELECT on ORDERS.ORDER_LINES). Granting WITH ADMIN OPTION (system privilege or role) or WITH GRANT OPTION (object privilege) lets the grantee pass it on.

Administrative privileges are SYSDBA, SYSOPER and, since 12c, the narrower SYSBACKUP, SYSDG and SYSKM (also SYSASM, SYSRAC). They authenticate through the password file or OS group membership, and SYS must connect with one of these clauses.

Separation of duties: SYSBACKUP is for backup and recovery (RMAN), SYSDG for Data Guard, SYSKM for encryption key management; each maps to an OS group on install, so one person need not hold SYSDBA to do one job.

Profiles set password and resource limits such as FAILED_LOGIN_ATTEMPTS, PASSWORD_LIFE_TIME, PASSWORD_LOCK_TIME and PASSWORD_VERIFY_FUNCTION; the DEFAULT profile applies unless another is assigned. Oracle ships verify functions (e.g. ORA12C_VERIFY_FUNCTION and ORA12C_STRONG_VERIFY_FUNCTION). Password-complexity errors surface as ORA-28003.

Unified auditing (the audit trail read through UNIFIED_AUDIT_TRAIL) records into one place; policies are made with CREATE AUDIT POLICY and switched on with AUDIT POLICY. In a new 19c database ORA_SECURECONFIG and ORA_LOGON_FAILURES are enabled by default; mandatory audit of things such as SYSDBA actions and audit configuration cannot be turned off.

Unified audit records are stored in SYSAUX by default; Oracle recommends moving the audit trail to its own tablespace and managing purge with DBMS_AUDIT_MGMT. Standard auditing (unified auditing itself) needs no extra license; Fine-Grained Auditing is Enterprise Edition.

Privilege analysis (DBMS_PRIVILEGE_CAPTURE) records which privileges are actually used, to find unused grants; capture types are database-wide, role, context or combination; a policy must be disabled before the report is generated; CAPTURE_ADMIN is needed. Check the Licensing Information manual for your edition before using it.

Transparent Data Encryption keeps its master key in a keystore (wallet) outside the database; the keystore is created and opened with ADMINISTER KEY MANAGEMENT; an auto-login keystore reopens on restart without a typed password; V$ENCRYPTION_WALLET shows its status. WALLET_ROOT and TDE_CONFIGURATION are set for the file keystore. Losing the keystore means encrypted data cannot be read, so back it up apart from the data.
Native network encryption and TLS are covered in the connectivity chapter; TDE protects data at rest in datafiles and backups, not data in memory or what an authorized user selects.

Credentials in scripts: avoid passwords on the command line (visible in process lists and shell history); use OS authentication, a secure external password store wallet, or an operator-prompted secret. A wallet-based external password store lets a script connect with a stored alias.

In a CDB, common users (names start with C## by default) live in the root and can have privileges in every container; local users live in one PDB. A privilege granted locally applies only in that container; with CONTAINER=ALL from the root it applies in all. Each PDB keeps its own local users, roles and profiles; unified audit policies can be common or local.

Oracle-supplied accounts (SYS, SYSTEM and sample or feature accounts) should be locked or have changed passwords; DBA_USERS.ACCOUNT_STATUS shows OPEN, LOCKED, EXPIRED. DBA_USERS.ORACLE_MAINTAINED = 'Y' marks Oracle-supplied accounts.
Views to verify effective access: DBA_SYS_PRIVS, DBA_TAB_PRIVS, DBA_ROLE_PRIVS, DBA_USERS, DBA_PROFILES, V$PWFILE_USERS, SESSION_PRIVS, SESSION_ROLES; CDB_ versions from the root show all containers.
PUBLIC is a role-like grantee that every user has; anything granted to PUBLIC is granted to all. Definer's-rights code runs with its owner's privileges, so EXECUTE on it lends the owner's reach.

snippets.code:
CREATE PROFILE svc_app LIMIT
  FAILED_LOGIN_ATTEMPTS 5
  PASSWORD_LOCK_TIME 1/24
  PASSWORD_LIFE_TIME UNLIMITED
  SESSIONS_PER_USER 40;
snippets.note: profile for a service account; syntax per 19c SQL Reference; lab values are placeholders
least-privilege app account; the password is a placeholder to be supplied from a secret store

snippets.code:
SELECT grantee, privilege, admin_option FROM dba_sys_privs WHERE grantee='ORDERS_APP'
UNION ALL SELECT grantee, granted_role, admin_option FROM dba_role_privs WHERE grantee='ORDERS_APP';
snippets.note: effective grants, direct and through roles one level

snippets.code: SELECT username, account_status, profile FROM dba_users WHERE oracle_maintained='N' ORDER BY username;

pitfalls: Granting DBA, or a handful of ANY privileges, 'to make the error go away' gives a service account the whole house.
A role is not active inside definer's-rights PL/SQL; privileges needed there must be granted directly.
The app owner (schema owner) and the app login are often one account; split them so the login cannot change the tables.
Locking an account is not the same as expiring a password; and expiring a service account's password in the night stops the shop (ORA-28001).
A password in a script or on the command line is visible to others on the host.
Encryption at rest does not stop an authorized user from selecting the data; and a lost keystore makes the backups unreadable.
Unified audit trail in SYSAUX grows unchecked unless purge is set up.
A privilege checked from the root can differ from what a PDB user has: always say which container.

rman-backup.note: Live fetches of docs.oracle.com were refused by the proxy on this pass; claims are standard 19c Backup and Recovery User's Guide behaviour from the build author's knowledge, cited to the guide, and should be re-checked against it (see volatile).

claims.text: Recovery objectives drive design: RPO is how much committed work you can lose, RTO is how long recovery may take. RMAN can only get you to the newest point for which you still hold both a backup and every archived redo log after it.

Recovery to any point after a backup (beyond restoring to backup time) needs ARCHIVELOG mode; in NOARCHIVELOG mode online redo is overwritten and only consistent, closed-database backups restoring to backup time are possible. Enable with ALTER DATABASE ARCHIVELOG from MOUNT state.

RMAN backs up datafiles, control file, SPFILE and archived redo logs. Backup sets are RMAN-format files holding only used blocks and can be compressed/encrypted; image copies are bit-for-bit copies of files, usable directly (SWITCH TO COPY) with no restore step.

Level 0 incremental copies all used blocks and is the base for later incrementals (it is not the same as a FULL backup for strategy purposes, although it holds the same blocks). Level 1 differential (default) copies blocks changed since the last level 0 or 1; level 1 cumulative copies blocks changed since the last level 0.

Block change tracking (CHANGE TRACKING FILE) lets level 1 incrementals read only changed blocks instead of scanning every datafile. It is an Enterprise Edition feature; check your edition before planning around it.

Incrementally updated backups: BACKUP INCREMENTAL LEVEL 1 FOR RECOVER OF COPY WITH TAG 'x' DATABASE; followed by RECOVER COPY OF DATABASE WITH TAG 'x'; keeps an image copy rolling forward so a restore needs few archived logs.

CONFIGURE CONTROLFILE AUTOBACKUP ON backs up the control file and SPFILE after every backup and structural change, to a known name format, so RESTORE SPFILE / RESTORE CONTROLFILE FROM AUTOBACKUP works even when the control file and repository are lost. The default is OFF, so set it ON explicitly.

Retention policy is either RECOVERY WINDOW OF n DAYS or REDUNDANCY n (default REDUNDANCY 1); the two are exclusive. Backups beyond policy are marked OBSOLETE (REPORT OBSOLETE / DELETE OBSOLETE). EXPIRED means the catalog lists a file that CROSSCHECK could not find on media. Policy does not itself delete anything; deletion is manual or by the fast recovery area when space is needed.

With the control file as the repository, CONTROL_FILE_RECORD_KEEP_TIME (default 7 days) must exceed the recovery window or backup records can age out before they are judged; a recovery catalog (separate database) removes that limit and stores longer history.

A backup that is not archived-log-complete is useless for point-in-time recovery: DELETE ARCHIVELOG must be tied to a backup (BACKED UP n TIMES TO DEVICE TYPE) or an archivelog deletion policy, never an operating-system rm, or RMAN will not know.

Fast recovery area (DB_RECOVERY_FILE_DEST and DB_RECOVERY_FILE_DEST_SIZE) holds archived logs, backups, flashback logs; when full, archiving can stall (ORA-19809, ORA-19804) and the database hangs. Monitor V$RECOVERY_AREA_USAGE and V$RECOVERY_FILE_DEST.

Failure isolation: keep backups on storage separate from the datafiles and from the FRA on the same disk group; a copy only on the same array is not a backup against array loss. Multiplex or copy backups (BACKUP BACKUPSET / DUPLEXED) to a second place.

Validation levels: BACKUP VALIDATE DATABASE (reads files, checks for corruption, writes nothing), RESTORE DATABASE VALIDATE (reads backups to prove they can be restored, does not restore), RESTORE DATABASE PREVIEW, and a real restore to a separate host (or DUPLICATE) as the only full proof. Corruptions show in V$DATABASE_BLOCK_CORRUPTION.

Useful monitoring: V$RMAN_STATUS, V$RMAN_BACKUP_JOB_DETAILS (status, input/output bytes, start/end), V$BACKUP_SET, LIST BACKUP SUMMARY, REPORT NEED BACKUP, REPORT UNRECOVERABLE. RMAN exit status is non-zero when a script fails, so schedulers can alarm on it.

In a CDB, connect to the root and BACKUP DATABASE covers all containers; BACKUP PLUGGABLE DATABASE name covers one PDB; you can restore/recover one PDB without taking down the others. SYSBACKUP is the least-privilege administrative privilege for RMAN (connect target '/ as sysbackup').
Tempfiles are not backed up as data; they are recreated on open. Online (hot) backups of datafiles need ARCHIVELOG mode and need no BEGIN BACKUP commands when RMAN is used.

snippets.code:
SELECT status, input_type, ROUND(elapsed_seconds/60) mins, TO_CHAR(start_time,'YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI') started
  FROM v$rman_backup_job_details ORDER BY start_time DESC FETCH FIRST 10 ROWS ONLY;

pitfalls: Backups exist but no archived logs after them: you can restore only to backup time.
Deleting archived logs with rm; RMAN thinks they exist (EXPIRED after crosscheck).
Control file autobackup off, then the control file and SPFILE are lost with the host: you cannot find the backups to start.
Never restoring: a backup that was never tried is a hope.
Backups and archived logs on the same disk group as the data: one failure takes both.
Retention policy mistaken for deletion; the FRA fills anyway.
Block change tracking and incrementals assumed on Standard Edition 2.
BACKUP VALIDATE success taken as proof of restorability.

recovery-flashback.note: Searches confirmed flashback retention/restore-point/undo-guarantee facts. Other claims (instance recovery, RMAN restore/recover, PITR, PDB PITR, RECOVER TABLE, flashback table/recycle bin) are standard 19c Backup and Recovery guide behaviour from the author's knowledge; re-check exact syntax against the guide.

claims.text: Instance (crash) recovery is automatic at the next startup: SMON rolls forward from the online redo (cache recovery) then rolls back uncommitted work using undo. It needs no DBA action and no backup; it does not need archived logs.

Media recovery is the DBA-driven path: RESTORE brings files back from backup, RECOVER applies archived and online redo to roll them forward. A damaged datafile in ARCHIVELOG mode can be restored and recovered while the rest of the database stays open (offline that file or tablespace first).

Losing all control files: with autobackup on, STARTUP NOMOUNT, RESTORE CONTROLFILE FROM AUTOBACKUP, ALTER DATABASE MOUNT, RECOVER DATABASE, ALTER DATABASE OPEN RESETLOGS. If another multiplexed copy survives, copy it over the missing one and restart instead.

Point-in-time recovery restores datafiles from before the target, applies redo up to an SCN/time/log sequence (RUN { SET UNTIL TIME ...; RESTORE DATABASE; RECOVER DATABASE; }), then ALTER DATABASE OPEN RESETLOGS, which starts a new incarnation; backups of earlier incarnations remain usable. Whole-database PITR discards all later work in every table.

Flashback Database rewinds the whole database using flashback logs in the fast recovery area. Prerequisites: ARCHIVELOG mode, a fast recovery area, and ALTER DATABASE FLASHBACK ON. DB_FLASHBACK_RETENTION_TARGET (minutes) is a goal, not a guarantee; the window actually reachable is shown in V$FLASHBACK_DATABASE_LOG, and flashback logs may age out if the recovery area is under space pressure.

FLASHBACK DATABASE is run from MOUNT state and verifies that the required archived and online redo is available; the database is then opened with ALTER DATABASE OPEN READ ONLY to inspect or OPEN RESETLOGS to keep the result.

A normal restore point only lets you flash back within the retention target. A guaranteed restore point ignores the target, keeps flashback logs until explicitly dropped (DROP RESTORE POINT), and can consume considerable recovery-area space. It guarantees flashback logs only, not enough undo for flashback table or query.

Flashback Database cannot undo loss or shrink of a datafile, a restored or recreated control file, or physical datafile loss/corruption; those need restore/recover. It is not a substitute for backups.

Row-level flashback (Flashback Query, Flashback Version Query, FLASHBACK TABLE ... TO TIMESTAMP) relies on undo, so it works only within the undo that is still kept; UNDO_RETENTION is a minimum honoured only if space allows, unless the undo tablespace has retention guarantee. FLASHBACK TABLE needs ROW MOVEMENT enabled on the table.

FLASHBACK TABLE ... TO BEFORE DROP restores a dropped table from the recycle bin, with its indexes under system names; purged objects or ones dropped when the tablespace was under pressure may be gone. SYS-owned and SYSTEM-tablespace objects are not recycled.

RMAN RECOVER TABLE (12c+) rebuilds chosen tables to a point in time in an auxiliary instance and can import them with Data Pump, leaving the rest of the database untouched. It needs a usable backup chain and enough disk for the auxiliary instance.
Recovery into a separate environment: RMAN DUPLICATE (from backup, with UNTIL TIME/SCN) builds a copy elsewhere to inspect or extract data without touching production.

PDB point-in-time recovery: from the root, ALTER PLUGGABLE DATABASE x CLOSE, RUN { SET UNTIL TIME ...; RESTORE PLUGGABLE DATABASE x; RECOVER PLUGGABLE DATABASE x; }, ALTER PLUGGABLE DATABASE x OPEN RESETLOGS. Other PDBs stay open. Flashback Database on a PDB (via PDB restore points) exists in 19c but is more restricted; check the guide.

Corruption: BACKUP VALIDATE CHECK LOGICAL and V$DATABASE_BLOCK_CORRUPTION list damaged blocks; RMAN RECOVER CORRUPTION LIST (or RECOVER DATAFILE ... BLOCK) repairs them from backup and redo while the file is online. Find the cause (storage, memory) before assuming the fix is final.

Decision order: if the file/disk is gone or corrupt, restore and recover. If the data is wrong but files are fine, pick the smallest tool that reaches the moment: flashback query to read, flashback table/recycle bin for a table, RMAN RECOVER TABLE or a duplicate for a table outside undo reach, flashback database or PITR when everything must go back. Always note the SCN/time before changing anything.

snippets.note: 19c; FLASHBACK ON can be run with the database open from 11.2.

snippets.code:
ALTER TABLE orders ENABLE ROW MOVEMENT;
FLASHBACK TABLE orders TO TIMESTAMP SYSTIMESTAMP - INTERVAL '30' MINUTE;

snippets.note: run connected to the CDB root

pitfalls: Writing down the SCN/time before acting; rewinding past the mistake loses good work.
Flashback logs age out under recovery-area pressure; a retention target is a goal.
Guaranteed restore point left in place fills the recovery area and freezes the database.
Flashback Database used for a lost datafile: does not work.
Whole-database PITR chosen when one table needed saving: loses everyone else's later work.
OPEN RESETLOGS run before looking (READ ONLY first) so a wrong target cannot be corrected.
Row flashback fails with ORA-01555 when undo has been reused.
Forgetting a fresh backup after RESETLOGS.

observability-troubleshooting.note: Web searches confirmed ASH, V$DIAG_ALERT_EXT and ADRCI/IPS facts (docs for 12.2/21c pages; 19c behaviour is the same). View/column names for V$SESSION, V$SESSION_WAIT classes, V$SYSTEM_EVENT, V$SQL, V$LOCK, V$SESSION_LONGOPS, V$SYSMETRIC, V$OSSTAT, V$PGASTAT, V$RECOVERY_FILE_DEST are standard 19c Reference content from the author's knowledge; re-check against the 19c Database Reference.

claims.text: The data dictionary (DBA_/ALL_/USER_ views) describes what exists and is stored; dynamic performance views (V$, GV$ on RAC) show what is happening now, are read from memory structures and the control file, and reset at instance restart.

V$ACTIVE_SESSION_HISTORY holds once-per-second samples of sessions that are on CPU or waiting on a non-Idle event; most of its columns mirror V$SESSION. Samples are kept in memory and a subset is flushed to AWR (DBA_HIST_ACTIVE_SESS_HISTORY). ASH and AWR need the Diagnostics Pack licence on Enterprise Edition.
V$DIAG_ALERT_EXT exposes the XML alert log in the ADR for the current container as rows, so the alert log can be queried with SQL; the plain-text alert_<SID>.log sits in the ADR trace directory.

ADRCI is the command-line tool to view diagnostic data and Health Monitor reports and to package incident data for Oracle Support using the Incident Packaging Service (IPS); a package is a logical construct until a file is generated from it.

V$SESSION shows each session's STATUS, SQL_ID, EVENT, WAIT_CLASS, SECONDS_IN_WAIT/WAIT_TIME_MICRO, BLOCKING_SESSION and FINAL_BLOCKING_SESSION; a waiting session's blocker is found by following BLOCKING_SESSION to the root.

A wait event is the database recording what a session is waiting for instead of running on CPU; events are grouped in wait classes (User I/O, Concurrency, Application, Commit, Configuration, Network, Idle). Application-class waits such as 'enq: TX - row lock contention' point to application design; 'log file sync' points to commit cost.
Time in the database is DB time = CPU time + non-idle wait time; the useful question for slowness is where DB time goes, not which counter is biggest.
V$SESSION_LONGOPS reports progress (SOFAR, TOTALWORK) for long operations such as full scans, sorts and RMAN jobs, which gives an honest estimate of time left.

Space-pressure symptoms: a full fast recovery area (V$RECOVERY_FILE_DEST, V$RECOVERY_AREA_USAGE) can stall the database because archiving cannot proceed; a full tablespace raises ORA-01653/01654; temp exhaustion raises ORA-01652.
Baselines make 'slow' measurable: compare AWR snapshots or metric history from a good period with the bad period; without Diagnostics Pack, Statspack is the free alternative.
claims.note: Statspack as free alternative is from author knowledge

claims.text: Before any configuration change, capture evidence (time, SCN, top waits, top SQL_IDs, alert log excerpt, OS load) so the change can be judged against it and rolled back.

snippets.code: SELECT wait_class, COUNT(*) sessions FROM v$session WHERE status='ACTIVE' AND type='USER' GROUP BY wait_class ORDER BY 2 DESC;
snippets.note: 19c; WAIT_CLASS shows 'Idle' for idle waits, ON CPU sessions show state WAITED... use STATE column to distinguish

snippets.code: SELECT sid, serial#, blocking_session, final_blocking_session, event, sql_id, seconds_in_wait FROM v$session WHERE blocking_session IS NOT NULL;
SELECT originating_timestamp, message_text FROM v$diag_alert_ext WHERE originating_timestamp > SYSTIMESTAMP - INTERVAL '1' HOUR ORDER BY originating_timestamp;
SELECT event, COUNT(*) samples FROM v$active_session_history WHERE sample_time > SYSDATE - 15/1440 GROUP BY event ORDER BY 2 DESC FETCH FIRST 5 ROWS ONLY;

adrci> show alert -tail 50
adrci> show incident
adrci> ips create package incident 12345
adrci> ips generate package 1 in /tmp
snippets.note: IPS flow; incident number is an example

pitfalls: Reading one view and calling it a diagnosis; the V$ view is a snapshot, not a history.
Using ASH/AWR/ADDM on Enterprise Edition without the Diagnostics Pack licence.
Killing the blocked session instead of finding the root blocker.
Treating high CPU as proof of a CPU problem when sessions mostly wait.
Restarting the instance to 'fix' slowness, which erases V$ evidence.
Changing three parameters at once so the cause of the improvement is unknown.
Forgetting that in a CDB, V$ views show per-container or CDB-wide data depending on where you are connected; CDB_ views differ from DBA_ views.

performance-sql.note: Web searches returned secondary sources for DBMS_XPLAN and licensing; core optimizer/trace facts are standard 19c SQL Tuning Guide content from the author's knowledge. Re-check against the 19c SQL Tuning Guide and Licensing Information manual.

claims.text: EXPLAIN PLAN shows the estimated plan without running the statement; DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY_CURSOR shows the plan a cursor in the shared pool actually used. With the GATHER_PLAN_STATISTICS hint (or STATISTICS_LEVEL=ALL) and FORMAT 'ALLSTATS LAST', it adds Starts, E-Rows, A-Rows and A-Time per plan step.

A large gap between E-Rows (estimated) and A-Rows (actual) at a plan step is the main sign of bad cardinality estimates, usually stale or missing statistics, skew, or correlated predicates; wrong cardinality leads to wrong access path and join method.

Optimizer statistics (table, column, index; histograms for skew) are gathered with DBMS_STATS, not ANALYZE; 19c has an automatic statistics-gathering maintenance task, and stats can be locked or restored from history.

Main access paths: full table scan, index range/unique scan, index fast full scan. Main join methods: nested loops (few outer rows, indexed inner), hash join (large unsorted inputs, equality), sort-merge. A full scan is not automatically bad.

A hard parse (new cursor built, optimizer runs, shared-pool latches taken) is costly; a soft parse reuses a cursor. Statements that differ only in literals are different cursors under CURSOR_SHARING=EXACT (the default), so applications should use bind variables.

CURSOR_SHARING=FORCE makes the database replace literals with system binds as a workaround for applications that cannot be changed; Oracle's optimizer blog warns it can leave one plan per statement and should be tested. Adaptive cursor sharing lets a bind-using statement get several child cursors when bind values change the best plan, visible in V$SQL (IS_BIND_SENSITIVE, IS_BIND_AWARE).
Every index speeds some reads but must be maintained on each insert, delete and key update, so extra indexes slow writes and add redo, undo and space. Index only what a measured statement needs.

Sorts and hash joins use work-area memory from the PGA; when a work area is too small the operation spills to temp (one-pass or multi-pass), shown in plans as TempSpc and in V$SQL_WORKAREA / V$PGASTAT. PGA_AGGREGATE_TARGET sets the instance-wide target.

SQL trace (DBMS_MONITOR.SESSION_TRACE_ENABLE with waits) writes a trace file per session to the ADR trace directory; TKPROF summarises it per statement into parse, execute and fetch counts, CPU, elapsed time, rows, and wait events.

AWR snapshots (hourly by default, 8-day retention by default) and ASH samples support reports (awrrpt.sql), ADDM and compare-periods work. AWR, ASH and ADDM need the Diagnostics Pack on Enterprise Edition; the SQL Tuning Advisor and SQL Access Advisor need the Tuning Pack. Statspack is the free alternative. CONTROL_MANAGEMENT_PACK_ACCESS (default DIAGNOSTIC+TUNING) controls pack access; setting NONE does not erase past usage recorded in DBA_FEATURE_USAGE_STATISTICS.

Honest measurement: compare before and after on the same data volume, with warm and cold caches considered, using logical reads (buffer gets), elapsed time and rows, repeated several times; a second run is faster partly because blocks are cached, so fewer disk reads alone does not prove the change worked.

snippets.code:
SELECT /*+ gather_plan_statistics */ COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE status = 'OPEN' AND customer_id = :cid;
SELECT * FROM TABLE(DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY_CURSOR(NULL, NULL, 'ALLSTATS LAST'));
snippets.note: run in the same session straight after the statement; 19c

snippets.code: EXEC DBMS_STATS.GATHER_TABLE_STATS(USER, 'ORDERS', cascade => TRUE);
SELECT sql_id, executions, parse_calls, buffer_gets, elapsed_time/1e6 secs FROM v$sql WHERE sql_text LIKE '%ORDERS%' ORDER BY elapsed_time DESC;

pitfalls: Reading EXPLAIN PLAN as proof of what ran; it is only the estimate.
Calling a full table scan or a high cost number the problem without checking A-Rows and time.
Adding an index for one query and slowing every insert.
Gathering stats at random and changing many plans at once; lock/restore history when needed.
Using AWR/ASH reports without the Diagnostics Pack.
Benchmarking a second, cached run against a cold first run.
